Once the key works again, after a passing **Test**, a save or an answer from Chat, the paused agents start again by themselves. If you remove the key, they start again on your plan's monthly AI limit.

Every admin is told once, with a notice at the top of their Chat **Inbox** and an e-mail. **Fix it** opens **Settings › AI Providers**. If the key still doesn't work 3 days later, they get one reminder. The notice goes away once the key works again, or is replaced or removed.

articles.title: Cancel your plan, or keep it after canceling

sections.text:
These options apply only when your deployment has billing enabled. Check the plans and terms shown in your workspace.

Canceling doesn't end your plan at once: it runs to the end of the period you've paid for, and every page says when it ends. Until then you can keep it with one click.

sections.heading: Cancel
sections.text: In **Settings › Billing**, an admin clicks **Cancel Subscription**. A short form asks what went wrong; both the reasons and the message are optional. You can also choose to give the team a few days to put it right, and your plan stays as it is meanwhile. **Send and cancel** cancels the plan at the end of the current period.

sections.heading: While the plan runs out
sections.text:
A thin band at the top of every page reads **Your plan ends on** and the date. For a canceled free trial, it says the trial ends on that date and the plan won't start.

An admin can click **Keep my plan** in the band: the plan renews as before, and the band goes. **Reactivate Subscription** in **Settings › Billing** does the same. Other members see a note to ask an admin.

The band's close button hides it in that browser tab. It comes back in a new tab, after the browser is closed, and when the plan is canceled to another date.

sections.heading: When the plan has ended
sections.text: Your workspace becomes read-only: you can look around, but adding, running and AI need a plan. Choose one from **See plans**.

articles.title: Set the rules Chat follows

sections.text: **Settings › Chat** holds the rules Chat follows in your workspace. Everyone can read them; only Admins change them. Each change counts from Chat's next step.

sections.heading: Run modes and tools
sections.text:
**Full auto** lets people run changes without a card. **Don't ask again** lets each person skip a card for one tool. Both need the Growth plan.

Under **Tool policy**, set each tool to **Never**, **Ask** or **Always**, within what the tool allows. **Reset to defaults** puts every tool back.

sections.heading: What Managers may take live
sections.text: Sending, publishing and other going-live steps always need a person's click. Turn a group off here, and a Manager gets **Ask your Admin** instead.

sections.heading: Agents that publish on their own
sections.text: Where your workspace has it, an Admin can let agents publish without a click. Turning it on opens a short dialog: tick that you understand and may decide this, then **Turn on**. Each agent then needs its own permission on its form, runs in **Full auto**, and goes live at most its daily limit. A page that fails Quality or your brand facts still waits for a click. It needs the Growth plan and Content Quality. Turning it off takes effect at once.

articles.title: Use GetCito in AI assistants with MCP

sections.text: GetCito has an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, so AI assistants such as Claude, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and Zed can query your GetCito data in a normal conversation. There is nothing to install: the assistant connects with an API key from **Settings › MCP & API Keys**.

sections.heading: Create an API key
sections.text:
1. Open **Settings › MCP & API Keys**.
2. Click **New key** and give it a name you'll recognize, such as "MCP — my laptop".
3. Click **Create** and copy the key. It's shown only once, so store it somewhere safe, such as your password manager.

sections.heading: Connect your assistant
sections.text:
The dialog that shows the key also has a ready-to-paste setup for each assistant under **Connect a client**, with the key filled in. Pick yours, click **Copy setup**, and follow the line under it, which says where the setup goes. Because it includes the key, copy it before you close the dialog.

In Claude's desktop app, for example, you add GetCito under **Settings › Connectors › Add custom connector**. On Claude's Team and Enterprise plans, an owner adds the connector in the organization settings first.

On a self-hosted install, the assistant connects to your own GetCito instead.

sections.heading: Check the connection
sections.text: Ask your assistant "List my GetCito brands". It should show your brands. If it reports a 401 error, the key is missing from the setup or was revoked.

sections.heading: What you can ask
sections.text:
Ask in plain words, for example:

- "What's my visibility score on ChatGPT for the last 7 days?"
- "Which topic has the most prompts?"
- "Who are my top 5 competitors by mention count this month?"
- "Why did our sentiment drop on Gemini?"

The assistant can read visibility, mentions, citations, prompts, AI traffic, saved reports, content, Site Audits, product visibility and the Action Center. Some requests change data, such as accepting a suggested prompt, writing a content draft or recording a task's progress. Assistants are told to make a change only when you ask for it.

sections.heading: What your plan includes
sections.text: In cloud mode, every plan can read over MCP, the free trial included. Changes, runs and anything that uses credits, such as accepting a suggestion, writing a content draft or starting a Site Audit, need the Growth plan or above, paid. On Starter and in the free trial, the assistant still sees those requests, but GetCito refuses them and says they need Growth, so it can tell you why. The same applies to the API and to every assistant: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and the others. An admin can upgrade in **Settings › Billing**. A self-hosted instance can do everything.

sections.heading: What your key may do
sections.text:
A key acts as the person who created it, with their role. Reading, drafts and suggestions in the Content Editor, Site Audits, task progress and an opportunity's progress are open to every role.

Adding prompts or topics, reviewing tasks, dismissing, and work that costs AI, such as content briefs and Improve actions, are for admins and managers. Dismissing a prompt suggestion is open to analysts too. Anything a role can't do is refused before it changes anything.

sections.heading: Publish a draft from your assistant
sections.text: GetCito never sends a page to your CMS through MCP. Instead, the assistant can get a draft as a page ready for your CMS, put it there with its own CMS connector, and then mark the draft published at the address it went live at, so GetCito measures it.

sections.heading: When the plan has ended
sections.text: In cloud mode, a workspace without an active plan is read-only. Its API keys keep working for reading, but every change is refused until an admin chooses a plan in **Settings › Billing**. Retrying doesn't help. New API keys can still be created; on a read-only workspace they only read. A self-hosted instance is never read-only.

sections.heading: Revoke a key
sections.text: If a key leaks or you stop using an assistant, open **Settings › MCP & API Keys** and click the trash icon next to the key. Assistants using it lose access immediately.

articles.title: Choose who sees which menu sections

sections.text: **Menu access** in Settings decides which sections are on each person's left menu, so everyone sees the part of GetCito they use. It only hides: a section off someone's menu still opens from a link, and what their role can do there doesn't change. To change what someone can do, change their role in **Settings › Team**.

sections.heading: Fold a group on your menu
sections.text: Click a group's title on the left menu, **Execution** or **Analytics**, to fold it, and again to open it; the arrow on its right shows which. This browser remembers it, and a folded group opens by itself when you go to one of its pages. **Chat** and **Agent Center** sit above the groups, and **Reports** and **Competitors** below them, so they don't fold.

sections.heading: Who can change menus
sections.text:
Admins change menus, and can let managers do it too: under **Who can change menus**, switch a manager on. That manager then sees **Menu access** in Settings, and nothing else of the admins' settings. They change what each role sees and every non-admin's menu, never an admin's.

Only admins choose who changes menus. A manager who becomes another role stops changing menus.

sections.heading: Choose what each role sees
sections.text:
**Sections each role sees** lists the left menu's sections, by group, with a column for each role. Tick what a role sees; each box is saved as you click it.

- **Admin** always sees **Everything**.
- **Action Center** is on everyone's menu and can't be turned off.
- **Use a set…** fills a role's column from a work area's ready-made set, or **Everything**. Adjust it from there. **Agent Center** is in every set: right after Chat where the set has Chat, else right after Action Center.

Until an admin hides something, every role sees every section.

sections.heading: Change one person's menu
sections.text:
**People** lists everyone but the admins, with their role, the work areas they picked, their menu and how many sections it keeps. A menu reads like **Analyst's menu**, or **Custom: +Prompts, −Content** when it differs from their role's.

Click **Customize** to tick or untick a section for that person alone, even one their role hides. Each change is marked **shown for them** or **hidden for them**, and saved as you click. **Use Analyst's menu**, named after their role, takes their changes back.

sections.heading: How a menu is worked out
sections.text:
A person's menu is their role's sections, changed by their own exceptions from **People**, then narrowed to the sections of their work areas, when they picked any.

**Action Center** always stays, and nobody takes a section off an admin's menu; only an admin's own work areas narrow it. A section added to GetCito later is on everyone's menu until someone hides it.

articles.title: Your free trial's AI credit, and starting your plan now

sections.text:
These options apply only when your deployment has billing enabled. Check the plans and terms shown in your workspace.

During the free trial, the AI features share a starter AI credit: Improve suggestions, the Content Editor's AI, the Action Center's task writing, and Chat where it's on. The credit is smaller than a plan's monthly AI usage, so the app shows how far along it is in words, not as a percentage.

sections.heading: Where you see it
sections.text:
- The **AI** button at the top right of each page reads **Trial credit**, then **Almost used** from 80%, and **Used up** once it's spent. Click it to see what the credit covers and when the trial ends.
- The AI usage card in **Settings › Billing** shows the same, and so does the usage next to **Settings** in Chat's menu.
- From 80%, a note under the page header says the credit is almost used.

sections.heading: Start your plan now
sections.text:
Once the credit is almost or all used, an admin can click **Start my plan now**: in the note under the page header, in the AI button's panel, or in the Billing card. A dialog shows the plan, what your card is charged today and that the free trial ends now. There's nothing to type: the card you added for the trial is on file.

Click **Start my plan now** in the dialog. The trial ends, the card pays the plan's first period, and the plan's full monthly AI usage starts from zero. On a monthly plan, the first-month offer applies while it's on.

sections.heading: If the card is declined
sections.text: Nothing changes and the trial carries on. Click **Update card** in the message to change the card, then try again.

sections.heading: Members who aren't admins
sections.text: Only admins can start or buy the plan. Other members see a note to ask an admin instead of the button.

sections.heading: Once the credit is used up
sections.text: AI features stop until the plan starts, now or when the trial ends. Chat keeps working only where it runs on your workspace's own AI key: own keys come with the Enterprise plan, and a key saved before Chat was turned on for your workspace keeps running it for 30 days. Where Chat isn't turned on yet, Agent Chat on your own AI key keeps working.

articles.title: Brand what you send clients with white label

sections.text: **White label** in Settings is your agency's kit: your logo, main color, company name and a footer line, for what you send your clients instead of GetCito's look. Each brand can also have its client's logo, for the cover of that brand's reports.

sections.heading: Set up your kit
sections.text:
- **Logo**: click **Upload logo** and pick a PNG, SVG or JPG of up to 1 MB. It is saved as soon as it is up. **Replace** and **Remove** change it later. A wide logo on a transparent background works best.
- **Company name**: your agency's name, as your clients know it.
- **Main color**: pick it, or type its hex code, such as #1d4ed8. Leave it empty to keep GetCito's.
- **Report footer**: one line at the bottom of each page, such as your website. Leave it empty for none.

Click **Save changes**. **Preview** shows a report's first lines with your kit as you type.

sections.heading: When the kit is used
sections.text:
The kit is used once it has a company name or a logo, on a plan with white label; the section says whether it is in use. Until then, or if the workspace's plan no longer has white label, everything keeps GetCito's look and the kit stays saved.

A light main color, such as yellow, is hard to read as text on white paper. The rules and bars keep your color, and text set in it is darkened just enough to stay readable. The section warns you when that happens.

sections.heading: Where your kit appears
sections.text:
With the kit in use, a brand's reports carry it. The report's page opens with a cover: your logo (or your company name without one), "Prepared for" and the brand's name, and the client's logo when the brand has one.

**Download PDF** makes the PDF with the same cover, your main color on its rules and bars, your footer line at the bottom of each page, and your company name as its author. It no longer carries GetCito's footer or names GetCito as its author, and its file name starts with your company's name.

Downloads from the other pages, such as CSV files, Excel sheets and Word files, also start their names with your company's name instead of GetCito's, and a Word file names your company as its author. Emails keep GetCito's look for now.

sections.heading: Who can change it
sections.text:
Only admins change the kit; everyone else in the workspace sees it. Under it, the section says when it was last changed and by whom.

On a plan without white label, the section is locked and names the plan that has it. Admins see **Upgrade**, which opens Billing; everyone else is asked to turn to an admin.

sections.heading: Add a client logo to a brand
sections.text:
Open the brand's **Brand settings**. On the **General** tab, **Client logo** takes the client's logo for that brand, in the same formats as your own. It goes on the cover of the brand's reports, beside "Prepared for" and the brand's name.

Admins and managers upload, replace and remove it; everyone who can see the brand sees it. The demo brand has none.

articles.title: Pick your work areas

sections.text: Each person can say what they work on or lead. Their left menu then keeps only those areas' sections. Pick one or more; picking none keeps every section. **Settings** is always on the menu, with your API keys and MCP.

sections.heading: The work areas
sections.text:
- **Founders & leaders**: Action Center, Chat, Agent Center, Brand Visibility, Mentions, AI Referral Traffic, Reports, Competitors.
- **AEO/GEO & Audit**: Action Center, Agent Center, Content, Audit, Citations, AI Referral Traffic, Reports.
- **Content**: Action Center, Chat, Agent Center, Content, Prompts, Citations, Reports.
- **Brand & PR**: Action Center, Chat, Agent Center, Brand Visibility, Mentions, Citations, Reports, Competitors.
- **Growth**: Action Center, Chat, Agent Center, Brand Visibility, Prompts, Citations, AI Referral Traffic, Reports, Competitors.
- **Product Development**: Action Center, Chat, Agent Center, Brand Visibility, Prompts, Mentions, Product Visibility, Reports.
- **Business Development**: Action Center, Chat, Agent Center, Brand Visibility, Prompts, Mentions, Citations, Reports, Competitors.
- **Developers**: Action Center, Agent Center, Audit, Prompts, Citations, AI Referral Traffic, Reports.
- **Analytics**: Action Center, Agent Center, Brand Visibility, Prompts, Mentions, Citations, Product Visibility, AI Referral Traffic, Reports, Competitors.

sections.heading: When you're asked
Change your work areas
sections.text:
Change your answer any time in **Settings › Account › Your work areas**. It also shows your menu, and why a section is off it: **Hidden by your admin** or **Not in your work areas**.

When something is off your menu, the bottom of the sidebar says how much, such as **3 sections off your menu**, with **Change** leading to your work areas.

articles.title: Fix site audit issues

sections.text: An audit report doesn't only score a page: it writes fixes for what failed. Start with the **AI Recommendations**, then open the failing signals. When you've made your changes, click the re-run icon at the top of the report to audit the page again.

sections.heading: AI Recommendations
sections.text:
**AI Recommendations**, right under the score, collects the fixes written for this page, ordered by priority: **high**, **medium** or **low**. Each names the signal and says what to change in one sentence. Where it helps, it gives a ready-to-paste draft, such as a meta description, an H1, an opening paragraph, FAQ questions and answers or sources to cite, and code, such as an FAQ schema block.

Mechanical signals, such as HTTPS, the viewport tag, alt text or a video embed, keep their general fix.

sections.heading: Your input needed
sections.text:
Recommendations only use facts found on the page, or your brand's name, description and domains when the page is on one of your domains. A number, percentage or date found in neither, such as a statistic, is left out with its sentence, so there is nothing for you to research.

Only what your brand alone knows is left in square brackets for you, three at most in a recommendation: a customer's name, your price, your own result, such as [customer name], [price] or [your result]. Each is highlighted, marked **Your input needed**. Replace each one before you publish. Search the pasted text for an opening bracket first: a placeholder left in schema code tells AI engines nothing.

sections.heading: Copy drafts and code
sections.text: Each draft and code block has a copy icon in its corner. It copies the block exactly as shown, placeholders included, and a **Copied** message confirms it.

sections.heading: Send a page to the Action Center
sections.text:
On a page that fails checks, **Send to Action Center** sends the page and the checks it fails as one Fix action, without waiting for the nightly pass. Sent again while that action is open, it doesn't add another: a notice names the open action, with **Open**. Only a page's latest report can be sent; an older one offers **Open the latest report**.

Once you complete the action, it is judged by the page's next audit: the checks it failed now passing.

sections.heading: How audits feed the Action Center
Re-audit after you fix
sections.text: Only each page's latest audit counts. Once a new audit no longer fails a check, the Action Center stops reporting that page; an audit older than 90 days no longer counts either. Auto-audit also re-audits, in its next run, the pages whose Site Audit fix you completed in the Action Center.

articles.title: Read a site audit report

sections.text: Each audit has its own report. It opens right after you run an audit, or from a row on the **Pages** tab. It scores the page out of 100, breaks the score down by category and lists every signal checked. The icons at the top re-run the audit on the same page or delete it; **Delete audit** can't be undone.

sections.heading: Total score
sections.text: The gauge shows the page's score out of 100 and a grade: **Good** (70 and above), **Needs work** (40 to 69) or **Poor** (below 40). When the page was audited before, a badge beside the grade shows the change since then, such as "+8 since" that audit's date. Beside it are the number of signals that **passed**, raised **warnings** or **failed**, and how many of the 48 signals were evaluated.

sections.heading: Categories
sections.text:
**Category breakdown** scores each category out of 100, with how many of its signals were evaluated:

- **Structure** (25%): whether an AI engine can parse the page, such as heading hierarchy, FAQ schema, lists and tables, and alt text.
- **Content** (25%): whether the page answers its question directly and completely.
- **Authority** (20%): whether it reads as expert and sourced, such as author byline, citations, statistics and freshness.
- **E-E-A-T** (20%): experience, expertise and trust, such as case studies and author credentials.
- **Trust** (10%): crawl-time basics such as AI bot access in robots.txt, llms.txt, HTTPS, canonical URL and meta description.

sections.heading: How the score is worked out
sections.text:
A category's score is the average of its signals, and the total is the weighted average of the categories. A signal that couldn't be evaluated, shown as n/a, is left out, so it never lowers the score.

Most signals are read straight from the page, its robots.txt and its llms.txt. Thirteen, such as **Direct answer to query** and **Case study evidence**, are judged by an AI model that first works out what the page itself is about, so a page is never judged against a topic it isn't trying to cover. **Brand entity in Wikidata** looks your brand up in Wikidata.

sections.heading: Same page, same score
sections.text:
The AI keeps its verdict on each of its thirteen signals until the part of the page that signal reads changes, so a page audited again with no changes gets the same score. A page that changed is judged again only on the signals whose part changed.

If the AI checks can't run, the page keeps the verdicts of its last audit. A page with none, such as one audited for the first time, gets a partial score: the report says the AI checks couldn't run, and the score leaves them out and isn't compared with your other audits. A partial audit doesn't use one of your monthly audits.

sections.heading: Signals
Readability
sections.text:
**Readability** reads the page in its own language: the language the page declares, else the one its words are in. English is scored with Flesch Reading Ease: 50 to 70 passes, 30 to 49 and anything over 70 raise a warning, and under 30 fails, so a plain page is never failed for reading easily. Turkish is scored with Ateşman, and German, French and Spanish with their own formulas: their easy score or more passes. Other languages are read by sentence and word length, and Japanese, Chinese and Thai show n/a for now. The Content Editor scores a page the same way.

The finding shows the score with its formula and language, then its parts: words a sentence, syllables and letters a word, and words a paragraph, with about how many lines a paragraph takes on a phone.

sections.heading: First-person evidence
sections.text: **First-person evidence** counts the sentences told as "I" or "we": in Turkish also by their verb endings, such as "gezdik" or "düşünüyoruz". Two or more pass and one raises a warning. Quotes and stock phrases such as "Contact us" don't count. It's read in English and Turkish; pages in other languages show n/a for now.

sections.heading: Authority links
sections.text: **Outbound authority links** passes with links to 2 authority sites and warns at 1. Open it to see which sites counted, other sites the page links to that don't, and **What counts**: government and academic sites (.gov, .edu and their country forms, such as .gov.tr or .ac.uk), international bodies (any .int site, un.org, europa.eu…), reference and research sites (Wikipedia, doi.org, arXiv…), major news, and the sites your brand trusts. Add those in **Settings › Content**; **Edit in Settings** takes you there.

sections.heading: Product pages
sections.text: On a product page, one with Product structured data, **Product description opening** checks that the description's first 40 words, or 250 characters, name the product type and at least two key attributes, such as a measure, a material, a fit or a use. ChatGPT appears to read only about that much of a description when it matches products to a shopping question. The finding shows where the opening ends. Other pages show this signal as n/a.

articles.title: Run a site audit

sections.text: **Site Audit** checks how ready a page is to be cited by AI answer engines. It fetches the page, runs 48 signals in five categories, scores the page out of 100 and writes fixes for what failed. You find it in the sidebar under **Execution**, after **Content**. It is on every plan.

sections.heading: Start an audit
sections.text:
The field at the top of the Site Audit page is filled in with your brand's primary domain. Replace it with the page you want to check and click **Run Audit**.

You can audit any page: your own, or a competitor's page to see what it does better. Audits of other sites are listed with your pages but kept out of your site's score.

sections.heading: While it runs
sections.text: The report opens right away and follows the audit through its stages: **Fetching the page…**, **Analyzing 48 signals…** and **Generating AI recommendations…**. An audit usually takes about 30 seconds. If it is still running after two minutes, the page says **This audit is taking longer than expected.** Click **Check again** to look again.

sections.heading: Other ways to start an audit
Before a bulk audit
sections.text:
Audit selected, Audit all and Re-audit ask first. They list the pages and say how many of the month's audits they use.

Pages audited in the last 7 days are left out, since a page that hasn't changed scores the same. Untick **Leave out** to include them.

When fewer audits are left than pages, the most valuable go now (on Pages, the first in the list) and the rest wait for next month.

sections.heading: Auditing a page again
sections.text:
A page has one audit running at a time. Starting it again, from any of these places, opens the audit already running and uses no audit, however the address is written: with or without www, a last slash or a tracking parameter.

When a page was audited in the last 10 minutes, Site Audit asks first: **Open it** shows that audit, and **Audit again** starts a new one. Pages started together leave those out and say so, with **Audit again**.

sections.heading: Your monthly audits
sections.text: Each completed audit uses one of your plan's monthly audits. An audit still running already counts; a failed one doesn't. The **Audits this month** card shows what's left. Plans without a monthly limit show **Unlimited** on the card.

sections.heading: How auto-audit works
sections.text:
Auto-audit spends a quarter of your monthly audits on the top pages of the **Opportunities** tab, in five runs on days 1, 7, 14, 21 and 28 of your billing month. On a plan without a monthly limit, auto-audit is off until you turn it on.

Pages you fixed go first: a page whose Site Audit fix you completed in the Action Center in the last 30 days, and that hasn't been audited since, so the action's result says whether the fix took. Pinned pages come next. Pages audited in the last 30 days wait for a later run. After a run, a notice sums it up with **View pages**, and its audits show **Auto** in the Pages list.

sections.heading: Site Audit settings
sections.text:
**Settings**, at the top right of the Site Audit page, holds:

- **Auto-audit**: on or off for every brand in your organization. Turned off, all your monthly audits are yours to spend.
- **E-mail the team after each run**: a summary e-mail after each auto-audit run.
- **Excluded pages**: one path per line, where an asterisk stands for anything. These pages stay out of Opportunities and auto-audits.
- **Pinned pages**: the pages you pinned from Opportunities, with **Unpin**.

Only admins and managers can change auto-audit, the e-mail and excluded pages; other members see them read-only.

articles.title: Site Audit scores, opportunities and pages

sections.text: The **Site Audit** page sums up your audits: a summary line, four cards and a chart, then two tabs. **Opportunities** lists the pages worth auditing next, and **Pages** lists every page you audited.

sections.heading: Summary and cards
sections.text:
A summary line gives your site score, pages audited, lowest category and next auto-audit. The first three cards count only the pages of your primary domain:

- **Site score**: the average score of each page's latest audit, and its change from each page's previous audit.
- **Pages audited**: how many of your site's pages, as your sitemap, Google Analytics and AI citations list them, have an audit from the last 90 days, and how many don't. **See the … not audited** opens those in Opportunities.
- **Authority · E-E-A-T**: those two category scores averaged over your pages, and the signals that fail or warn on the most pages.
- **Audits this month**: audits left this billing month, with the share auto-audit keeps for its next runs.

sections.heading: Score over time
sections.text:
**Score over time** charts your primary domain's audit scores, one point a day from the latest audit that day, over 7d, 30d, 90d or All. The category breakdown of the latest audit sits beside it. The chart needs audits on at least two days.

With the Content Editor's Quality on, a **Site trust** card, out of 5, reads your site's trust pages. It counts toward Quality's Trust, not the audit score.

sections.heading: Why a page is in Opportunities
Priority and templates
sections.text:
The priority multiplies the page's value to the business, the size of the opportunity and how easy it is to fix, meaning how close its last score is to passing. Hover the number to see the three parts.

Pages built from one template, such as every post of a blog, share most of their gaps. When at least two-thirds of a template's audited pages fail or warn on the same signals, the template gets one row: **Fix once, applies to** its pages. Auditing it audits the template's pages that have no audit yet.

sections.heading: Select, pin or exclude
sections.text:
Select rows to **Audit selected**, to **Pin** them, so they always come first, or to **Exclude** them. Excluded pages are listed under the table, where **Restore** puts them back.

Pins and exclusions hold for the whole brand, so only admins and managers see **Pin**, **Exclude** and **Restore**.

sections.heading: The Pages tab
sections.text:
**Pages** lists every page you audited, one row per page, most recent first, with its **First score**, **Current score**, **Issues** (signals that failed or warned), **Status** and **Last audit**. Once a page has two audits, the change since the first shows beside the current score: green up, red down. Status is **Good** (70 or more), **Improving** (below 70 but up from the previous audit), **Needs work**, **Running** or **Failed**. **Auto** marks an auto-audit's audit.

Click a row to open its latest report. The arrow beside a page lists its earlier audits, each with **View report** and a delete icon. **Group by template** groups the rows under their template. **Export** downloads the list as CSV or Excel, first scores included; select pages to **Re-audit** them or export only those.

articles.title: Brand Visibility page overview

sections.text: **Brand Visibility** in the sidebar opens **Answer Engine Insights**, the main analytics page for a brand. It's your daily view of how AI answers treat your brand across your tracked prompts, and where to act next.

sections.heading: The header
sections.text:
The header shows the brand's name, when the last run finished and when the next one is due. It has these buttons:

- **Formulas** explains how every number on the page is calculated.
- **Export CSV** downloads the answers behind the page, with the current filters.
- **Reports** opens the Reports page.

A self-hosted instance also has **Test Single Prompt** and **Run All**, to start a run by hand.

sections.heading: The summary line
sections.text: Below the filters, one line sums up your Visibility score and its change, your rank and the gap to the brand next to you, and the platforms that moved most. The copy button puts the line on your clipboard, ready to paste into a message or a report.

sections.heading: The key metric cards
sections.text:
Nine cards follow. Most show their change **vs previous period** and a small daily line:

- **Visibility**: your score from 0 to 100, and your rank among the tracked brands, or, before you track competitors, how many prompts you appeared in. Click it to open the **Visibility Breakdown** panel.
- **Tracked prompts**: the prompts answered in the period. On plans with a limit, a bar shows how many prompt locations your workspace uses. Click it to open Prompts.
- **Mentions** and **Citations**: how often answers named your brand and cited your pages. They open the Mentions and Citations pages.
- **Net sentiment**: the positive minus the negative share of the answers that name you. It opens Mentions.
- **Coverage**, **Share of voice**, **Avg. position** and **Citation rate**.

A rate based on fewer than 20 answers says **Low sample** and shows no change.

sections.heading: Visibility trend
sections.text:
The trend and the Leaderboard are shown once you track competitors; until then, a card links you to adding them.

The trend draws your Visibility over the date range next to your competitors' lines. Admins and managers can **Pin** up to 5 competitors to keep on the chart; without pins, the strongest four are shown. Outside the 24-hour view, the chart also marks the days prompts were added and your Action Center goal for AI visibility, if one is set.

sections.heading: Leaderboard
sections.text:
The **Leaderboard** ranks you against your competitors, with each brand's score, change, Coverage and share of voice. Under your row it shows the gap to the brand ahead and the platform where that brand leads you most.

**Head-to-Head** opens the **Competitors** page. A competitor's name opens it with that competitor selected. Before a brand has competitors, **Head-to-Head Comparison** appears in the Leaderboard's place and opens the same page.

sections.heading: By AI platform
sections.text:
**By AI platform** is a table with each platform's **Visibility**, **Change**, **Coverage**, **Share of voice** and **Avg. pos**. The row with the biggest drop is highlighted.

A platform with too few answers shows **Low sample** or **No runs this period** instead of numbers. Use the table to send your content work toward your weakest platform.

sections.heading: Why it changed
sections.text:
**Why it changed** lists the platforms, topics and prompts that moved your Visibility most, under **Gains** and **Drops**. Each row shows its own score before and after, and its effect on your overall score. A note counts the prompts added during the period, which aren't counted in the change.

Click a row, or **Full breakdown**, to open the **Visibility Breakdown** panel.

sections.heading: Topics vs competitors
sections.text: **Topics vs competitors** has one row per topic, with your score and the score of each competitor on the trend, shaded from low to high. The last column shows the gap to the topic's leader, or **Lead** when you lead. Click a topic to open its page.

sections.heading: Opportunities
sections.text:
**Opportunities** shows what to track next, from your prompt suggestions:

- A topic has **Track N**, which tracks all its suggested prompts, and **Send action**, which opens a Growth action in the Action Center.
- A prompt has **Track**, and **Suggest content**, which writes a content suggestion for its topic from your monthly content allowance.

Tracking stops when your plan's prompt locations are full. **Track**, **Track N** and **Suggest content** are for admins and managers. **See all** opens **Prompt Suggestions** under **Prompts**.

sections.heading: Volumes on Opportunities
sections.text: The volumes shown with these suggestions are an AI's guess, since no keyword behind them is measured yet. They are always low confidence: grey, from half to twice the guess. Track a prompt to get an estimate from its keywords' Google searches.

sections.heading: Filters and date range
sections.text:
Under the header:

- **Date Range**: **24h** (the default, the latest completed run), **7d**, **30d**, **90d**, **All** or **Custom**.
- **Topic**: one topic, shown when the brand has topics.
- **Region**: one region your prompts run in.
- **AI Model**: one AI platform; versions of the same engine count as one.

The filters apply to everything on the page except **Opportunities**, which lists your stored suggestions. They're kept in the page's address, so a link you share opens with the same filters.

sections.heading: A weekly review
sections.text:
1. Set the range to **7d**. Is your Visibility up or down? If it's down, **Why it changed** shows which platforms, topics and prompts moved it.
2. In **By AI platform**, find the platform with the lowest score or the highlighted biggest drop: that's your next investment.
3. Look at the suggested topics and prompts in **Opportunities**, and track one to three of them.
4. From **Opportunities** under **Content** in the sidebar, open the opportunity for the topic that did worst this week and click **Generate Brief**.

articles.title: What visibility, position, mentions and citations mean

sections.text: GetCito describes how AI answers treat your brand with a few metrics: visibility, mentions, citations, position and the rates built on them. They are counted from real AI answers, not estimated, so they never carry an **Estimate** badge.

sections.heading: Read your visibility score
sections.text:
Visibility is a score from 0 to 100, not a percentage. It blends how often AI answers mention your brand, how often they cite your site and how early they name you; **Formulas** on **Brand Visibility** shows the exact formula. A rough guide, not bands the app shows:

- **Under 15**: cold start. AI engines barely know the brand on these prompts.
- **15 to 35**: emerging presence. AI sometimes mentions you, but competitors dominate.
- **35 to 60**: established. You're reliably mentioned; focus on the one or two platforms or topics still trailing.
- **Over 60**: category leader. Your job is defending your place against new entrants.

The right threshold depends on how competitive the category is: in a crowded category, 20 can already be leadership.

sections.heading: Watch the change, not the number
sections.text:
Don't fixate on the absolute number; watch how it moves. A brand growing from 18 to 24 in a quarter is healthier than one stuck at 50.

Every change compares the selected range with the period of the same length just before it, over only the prompts answered in both. Visibility changes are in points; Mentions and Citations change in percent.

sections.heading: A score of 0
sections.text: A score of 0 doesn't mean something is broken. New, niche or B2B brands often start at 0 on most prompts. AI engines need either plenty of training data that mentions your brand or live citations from trusted sources, and the score stays at 0 only while both are missing.

sections.heading: Coverage, share of voice and the other rates
sections.text:
The key metric cards on **Brand Visibility** also show:

- **Coverage**: the share of answered prompts where you appear at least once.
- **Share of voice**: your mentions out of all mentions of tracked brands.
- **Avg. position**: where you're named in the answers that name you. Lower is better.
- **Citation rate**: the share of answers that cite your domain.
- **Net sentiment**: the positive minus the negative share of the answers that name you.

A rate based on fewer than 20 answers says **Low sample** and shows no change.

sections.heading: Position and Performance
sections.text:
Position is where your brand is named among the brands an AI answer lists; named earlier is better. The **Performance** filter in **Tracked Prompts** groups prompts by it, over the selected range and across every platform the prompt tracks:

- **Best**: named in the first third of the brands an answer lists.
- **Good**: in the middle third.
- **Late**: in the last third.
- **Missing**: named in fewer than half the answers.

A prompt with no answers in the range, such as a new one, has no performance yet. The **Positions** column shows your average position and its change; hover it for each platform.

sections.heading: Mentions and citations
sections.text:
A mention is each time an AI answer names your brand or your domain; one answer can add several. The **Mentions** card counts them. Mention detection ignores upper and lower case, so name the brand exactly as it's named in the wild, not by an abbreviation.

A citation is a source page that comes with an AI answer. The **Citations** card counts how often answers cited your pages, and the **Citations** page shows which domains and pages AI engines cite for your prompts.

sections.heading: Prompts that skew your metrics
sections.text: Prompts that include your brand name almost always score high, because the AI obviously talks about you when asked. They don't measure how AI engines discover you on their own, and they distort your averages, so keep tracked prompts free of your brand name.

articles.title: How the AI Visibility Score is calculated

sections.text: The **AI Visibility Score** is a score from 0 to 100, not a percentage. It blends three things over the answers in your date range and filters: how many answers name your brand, how many cite a page of yours, and how early you're named. A score of 0 means no answer names or cites you; the closer every answer comes to naming you first and citing you, the closer the score gets to 100. **Formulas** on **Brand Visibility** shows the exact formula.

sections.heading: The three parts
sections.text:
- **Mention rate (60%)**: the share of answers that name your brand.
- **Citation rate (25%)**: the share of answers that cite a page of yours.
- **Position (15%)**: how early you're named, in the answers that name you. Being named first counts 1, second a half, third a third, and so on, averaged. While only a few answers name you, this part counts for less, so one lucky first place can't lift the score on its own.

The score is 100 times the sum of 0.6 × mention rate, 0.25 × citation rate and 0.15 × the position part (reduced while few answers name you), to one decimal. All three parts read the same answers, so the filters you set apply to each of them.

sections.heading: Every answer counts
sections.text: Every answer counts, including the ones that leave you out. Competitors are scored the same way over the same answers, so their numbers are directly comparable with yours.

sections.heading: A single answer's score
Comparing periods
sections.text: The change shown beside a score, in green or red, compares your date range with the period before it, **vs previous period**. It uses only the prompts answered in both periods, so the comparison is like for like.

sections.heading: Where you see the score
sections.text:
- **Brand Visibility**: the brand's score, its trend and the change vs the previous period.
- **Tracked Prompts** under **Prompts**: each prompt's score.
- **Topics** under **Prompts**: each topic's score, and **Topics vs competitors** on Brand Visibility.
- **Competitors**: each tracked competitor's score beside yours.

sections.heading: What moves your score
sections.text:
Typical effects, not guarantees:

- Publishing a citation-friendly comparison page: up, over one to four weeks as AI engines re-index.
- Earning coverage on a major review or list site: up within two to seven days, often at once.
- Losing a press citation, such as a retracted article: down within a week.
- A competitor outpacing you with better structured data: your relative score declines.
- Adding new prompts to your tracked set: the score may dip until those prompts mature.

sections.heading: What doesn't move your score

articles.title: Find out why your visibility changed

sections.text: When your Visibility goes up or down on **Brand Visibility**, two parts of the page explain it: the **Why it changed** card and the **Visibility Breakdown** panel. Both compare the date range you picked with the period of the same length just before it.

sections.heading: How a change is measured
sections.text:
Every change compares the selected range with the period of the same length just before it, **vs previous period**, over only the prompts answered in both periods. Adding prompts doesn't inflate it.

Visibility changes are in points; Mentions and Citations change in percent. With **All** selected there is no earlier period, so no change is shown. A rate based on fewer than 20 answers says **Low sample** and shows no change.

sections.heading: The Why it changed card
sections.text:
**Why it changed** lists the platforms, topics and prompts that moved your Visibility most, under **Gains** and **Drops**. Each row shows its own score before and after, and its effect on your overall score. With **All** selected, the card doesn't show. When either period has fewer than 20 answers, it says there are too few answers to explain the change.

A note counts the prompts added during the period: they aren't counted in the change. Click a row, or **Full breakdown**, to open the **Visibility Breakdown** panel.

sections.heading: The Visibility Breakdown panel
sections.text:
The **Visibility** card, a row of **Why it changed** and **Full breakdown** all open the **Visibility Breakdown** panel. It compares the selected range with the period of the same length just before it, and names the prompt and platform behind the biggest gain or drop.

It lists every slice under three tabs: **Prompts**, **Platforms** and **Topics**. Click a prompt to open its page, where **Platform Results** shows each AI answer and the sources it cited.

sections.heading: Investigate a sharp drop
sections.text:
1. Click the **Visibility** card, or the dropped row in **Why it changed**. The panel names the prompt and platform behind the biggest drop.
2. Click the prompt to open its page and read the answers under **Platform Results**. Is your brand still mentioned but named later, or completely absent?
3. Check the competition: the **Leaderboard** and **Topics vs competitors** show who leads where. A competitor surge is often the cause; **Head-to-Head** opens the Competitors page for a closer look.
4. Check the sources each answer cited; the **Citations** card opens the Citations page. A retracted article or a new competitor post is often the trigger.

sections.heading: Decide what to do
